title: Reasoning models and reasoning effort
summary: Reasoning models spend hidden thinking tokens before they answer. An effort setting trades quality against latency and cost, and some sampling parameters are rejected.
useIf: You use a reasoning model, tune effort, or see 400 errors after switching models.
avoidIf: The task is simple extraction or classification where a small non-reasoning model passes your evals.

explain.md: A **reasoning model** generates internal thinking before the visible answer. Those **reasoning tokens** bill as output, share the context window, and appear in `output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` (Responses) or `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` (Chat Completions) [[r3]]. You cannot read the raw thinking. On OpenAI you receive a summary only if you ask for `reasoning.summary` (`auto`, `concise` or `detailed`).

**Effort** controls how much the model thinks. OpenAI uses `reasoning.effort` in Responses and `reasoning_effort` in Chat Completions. Anthropic uses `output_config.effort`, which is GA, with `thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}` so the model decides how much to think [[r31]]. Higher effort costs output tokens and latency, so start low and raise it only when evals show a gain. Verbosity (`text.verbosity` or `verbosity`, values `low`, `medium`, `high`) is a separate control over answer length.

explain.title: Sources disagree on rejected parameters
explain.md: OpenAI says that when effort is not `none` you should remove `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_logprobs`, plus `logprobs` in Chat [[r2]]. The Azure page lists a longer rejected set for reasoning models, yet its GPT-6 table marks `temperature`, `top_p` and `logprobs` as supported on all four GPT-6 models [[r15]]. Test your own deployment.

Other reasoning controls: `reasoning.mode` is `standard` (default) or `pro` on GPT-5.6 and GPT-6, independent of effort. `reasoning.context` is `auto`, `current_turn` or `all_turns`, and GPT-5.6 defaults to `all_turns`. A `configuration_update` input item changes effort mid-conversation without changing the cached prefix [[r3]].

whereToUse: Multi-step analysis, planning, math and code where a wrong first guess is costly
Agents that call tools in a loop and must recover from errors
Offline jobs where latency is irrelevant and accuracy pays, often through Batch or Flex
Interactive products at `low` effort when a small quality gain matters more than a few hundred milliseconds
Replacing complicated chain-of-thought prompts that the model handles internally

use: The task fails often with a non-reasoning model on your evals
Errors are expensive and latency budget is generous
The task needs planning across tool results
avoid: Classification, extraction and formatting where a small model already passes
Strict latency targets such as a spoken reply, unless effort is `none` or `low`
Code that relies on `temperature`, `top_p` or `logprobs` for behaviour
flips: Evals show no gain from `high` over `low`: stay at `low`
The cap leaves no room for thinking: raise `max_output_tokens` before raising effort
You move to GPT-6 Astra or 6.1 Sol: stop sending `none`, use `low` and re-evaluate

pitfalls.symptom: HTTP 400 after upgrading to GPT-6 Astra
pitfalls.cause: The code sends `reasoning.effort: none`, which Astra rejects
pitfalls.fix: Use `low` as the starting point and rerun evals

pitfalls.symptom: 400 for `temperature` or `top_p` on a reasoning call
pitfalls.cause: Sampling parameters are removed when effort is not `none`
pitfalls.fix: Drop them and steer with effort, verbosity, schemas and evals

pitfalls.symptom: Code that prints thinking text shows nothing on Claude Fable 5
pitfalls.fix: Set `thinking.display` to `summarized` if you need a summary

pitfalls.symptom: Bills rise while answers look the same length
pitfalls.cause: Hidden reasoning tokens bill as output
pitfalls.fix: Track reasoning tokens per request and cap with `max_output_tokens`

scenarios.title: Live chat, easy intent routing
scenarios.situation: A customer chat widget routes each message to one of eight queues. The team wants a 3 second p95 and low cost at high volume.
constraints: Wrong routes are cheap to fix
unknowns: Accuracy of a small model on the labelled set
scenarios.question: Which setup do you start with?

options.name: Large model at `xhigh` effort
options.why: It adds seconds and large cost for a narrow task that does not need deep reasoning.
options.tradeoff: It is right for rare, hard, high-stakes tasks with a loose latency budget.

options.name: Small non-reasoning model, or a small model at `low` effort, chosen by evals
options.why: A narrow label task fits a small model, and low effort keeps latency inside the budget.
options.tradeoff: A harder edge case may fail and need an escalation path.

options.name: Large model at `low` effort
options.why: Higher quality ceiling at modest latency.
options.tradeoff: Costs more per request than a small model that already passes.

flips.if: Misroutes are costly, for example legal escalation
flips.then: Add a cascade to a larger model for low-confidence cases.

flips.if: The small model misses the accuracy bar
flips.then: Raise effort or move up a model size and re-run evals.

scenarios.takeaway: Match effort to difficulty and latency, and let evals justify any increase.

scenarios.title: Overnight contract analysis
scenarios.situation: A legal team runs deep comparisons across contracts each night. Results are reviewed in the morning. Errors are costly and latency does not matter.
unknowns: Does `high` beat `medium` on a labelled set?
Which service tier is allowed for this data?
scenarios.question: How do you configure it?

options.name: `high` effort with a generous output cap, run through Batch or Flex for the 50% discount
options.why: Quality matters and latency does not, and Batch and Flex run at 50% of Standard [[r37]] [[r38]].
options.tradeoff: Jobs can take up to 24 hours, and Flex is Beta and may be unavailable.

options.name: `low` effort synchronously to save money
options.why: It saves tokens on the one workload where thinking pays, and stakes are high.
options.tradeoff: Low effort is right for latency-bound, easy tasks.

options.name: `high` effort synchronously at Standard price
options.tradeoff: Pays about twice the batch price for latency nobody needs.

flips.if: Data may not use Batch under your retention policy
flips.then: Run synchronously and accept the price.

scenarios.takeaway: When latency is free, spend it on effort and take the batch discount.

scenarios.title: 400 after a model upgrade
scenarios.situation: A service sets `reasoning.effort: none` for speed and `temperature: 0.2`. After switching the deployment to GPT-6 Astra it returns HTTP 400.
constraints: The service must keep working this week
unknowns: Does `low` effort meet the latency target?
scenarios.question: What do you do?

options.name: Retry the same request with a delay
options.why: The error is deterministic. The request is invalid for that model.
options.tradeoff: Retries suit 429 and 5xx errors, not validation errors.

options.name: Remove `temperature`, replace `none` with `low`, then rerun evals and a latency check
options.why: It fixes both rules at once and keeps the test loop.

options.name: Route this task to a model that supports `none`, such as GPT-6 Sol or Luna, and keep the controls
options.why: The task wanted no reasoning, and those models accept `none`, so quality and latency stay stable [[r2]].
options.tradeoff: You depend on a different model and must still drop `temperature` when effort is above `none`.

flips.then: Use `low` on Astra and tune from there.
Test each rejected parameter, since the pages disagree.

scenarios.takeaway: Treat a 400 as a contract change and read the model page.

quiz.q: A reasoning call returns `status: incomplete` with no visible text. What is the likeliest cause?
options: The output cap was consumed by reasoning tokens
quiz.explain: Reasoning tokens count against `max_output_tokens`, so a low cap can end the response before any text. Temperature and `store` do not produce this result, and a refusal is a different signal.

quiz.q: Which changes can justify raising reasoning effort?
options: Evals show a measurable gain on hard cases
The task is multi-step with tool results
Errors are expensive and latency is loose
quiz.explain: Gains on evals, multi-step tool tasks and costly errors justify more effort. A shorter answer is a verbosity setting, not an effort setting.

quiz.q: Code sends `reasoning.effort: none` to GPT-6 Astra. What happens?
quiz.explain: Astra accepts `low` to `max`, and `none` returns HTTP 400 [[r2]]. It does not fall back to another value.

flashcards.front: Where do reasoning tokens show up in usage?
flashcards.back: `output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` in Responses and `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` in Chat Completions. They bill as output.
GPT-6 Astra (HTTP 400) and GPT-6.1 Sol (no `none` or `minimal`). GPT-6 Sol and Luna accept `none` to `max`.

flashcards.front: What do you start with when tuning effort?
flashcards.back: Start low and raise only when evals show a gain, since effort adds output tokens and latency.

flashcards.front: What does Claude use instead of `budget_tokens` on new models?
flashcards.back: Adaptive thinking with `output_config.effort`. Manual `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and not accepted on later models.
